passage: Pradeep, since your podcast is about early careers, here's what changed things for me. Last year I was twenty-four, a junior analyst, and every night I'd scroll through batchmates' updates: promotions, startup funding, conference talks. I'd go to sleep feeling like a failure. So I tried something. I opened my work folder from a year earlier and put it next to this year's. A year ago I couldn't build a basic forecast model without help. Now I train the new joiners on it. That hit me. Then I muted about fifteen accounts that always left me low. Not blocked, just muted. And I picked three people, two seniors and one batchmate, whose work I actually want to learn from, and I ask each of them one question a month. I'm Siddharth, by the way. Twenty-five now, and much calmer.

qa.q: How many accounts did Siddharth mute?
qa.a: About fifteen accounts that always left Siddharth low.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel going to sleep after scrolling, a year ago?
qa.a: Siddharth felt discouraged, like a failure, measured against batchmates' promotions and funding.

qa.q: Which of Siddharth's choices keeps the useful side of comparison?
qa.a: Picking three people to learn from and asking each one question a month keeps comparison about learning, not ranking.

qa.q: How might the batchmate Siddharth chose to learn from feel about the monthly question?
qa.a: They would probably feel respected and pleased, seeing their work valued rather than competed with.

grounding: A young professional describes measuring progress against a past self, muting accounts that drag the mood down and choosing a few peers to learn from.

passage: I'm Pankaj. Hrithik and I joined the architecture firm together two years ago, and until recently he checked everyone's projects like a scoreboard. If someone else got a client presentation, he'd go quiet for a day. Lately he's different. Last week I saw him with two sketchbooks open on his desk: one from his first month, one from now. He was flipping between them and actually smiling. When I asked, he said, "Checking how far I've come, not how far they have." He told me he'd muted a few people online who "make me feel like trash for no reason". And he's started having lunch with Mrs Iyer, the senior who does the best site plans, asking her one thing each time. I can't tell what's going on inside him. He just seems lighter.

qa.q: What two sketchbooks did Hrithik have open?
qa.a: One from his first month and one from now.

qa.q: What might Hrithik's smile over the sketchbooks suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt quietly proud, seeing his own progress instead of measuring himself against others.

qa.q: Why is lunch with Mrs Iyer a better use of comparison than checking the scoreboard?
qa.a: It turns a stronger colleague into a teacher, so Hrithik learns specific skills rather than just feeling behind.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel working beside a lighter Hrithik?
qa.a: Pankaj probably finds him easier to be around, without the quiet days whenever someone else got a presentation.

grounding: A colleague notices a young architect shift to comparing with his own past work, muting draining accounts and learning from one senior.

passage:
January. Ankita scrolled through posts from her old college group late at night: new jobs abroad, a marathon medal, a wedding in the hills. She shut the laptop feeling like she'd wasted a year. Even Jyoti, her closest friend, seemed miles ahead.
February. On a Sunday she opened the note where she'd written her goals a year earlier: "learn the data tools, stop freezing in meetings, cook more at home." She ticked two out of three. Then she muted six accounts that always made her chest tight.
April. Now she meets Jyoti and one colleague for coffee every second Saturday, and they each swap one thing they've learned. Last time Jyoti asked how she'd got so much better at presenting. Ankita laughed. "I compared myself to January me."

qa.q: How many accounts did Ankita mute?
qa.a: Six accounts that always made her chest tight.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel after scrolling in January?
qa.a: She felt discouraged, as if she had wasted a year, with even Jyoti seeming miles ahead.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Checking last year's goals showed real progress, two out of three, and the coffee circle turned peers into people to learn from.

qa.q: How might Jyoti see the Saturday coffees?
qa.a: Jyoti seems to value them too, asking Ankita for presenting tips, so the learning runs both ways.

grounding: Over a few months a young professional stops measuring herself against others' highlights, checks her own past goals, mutes draining accounts and learns with a few peers.

passage: Anirban, you've refreshed that alumni group all morning. Sit with your old Deepak sir a minute. Fifteen years ago, twenty-five and new at this agency, I did the same. Every evening, batchmates' posts: Singapore, a startup, a car. I'd come in next day feeling like a failure. One Sunday I found my notebook from the year before, my first month's to-do lists. "Learn the layout software." "Don't freeze in client meetings." I laughed out loud. I'd done all of it. So I made a rule: once a month, I compared myself only with that notebook. I muted the six people whose posts always flattened me; didn't unfriend anyone, just stopped looking. And I picked two people, Farzana and old Mr Pillai, whose work I truly wanted to learn from, and asked them to lunch. That's the whole trick. Now, what's in your notebook from last year?

qa.q: How many people did Deepak mute?
qa.a: Six people, the ones whose posts always flattened Deepak.

qa.q: Why did Deepak laugh out loud at the old notebook?
qa.a: Deepak suddenly saw real progress: every worry from the year before, like the layout software and client meetings, had been handled.

qa.q: Which of Deepak's choices kept the useful side of comparison?
qa.a: Picking Farzana and Mr Pillai to learn from kept comparison as a teacher, while muting the six removed the part that only hurt.

qa.q: How might Anirban take the closing question about last year's notebook?
qa.a: Anirban may feel gently steered from the alumni group toward personal progress, without being told how to feel.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls measuring progress against the previous year, muting accounts that flattened the mood, and choosing a few peers to learn from.

passage: Rustam's self-appraisal was due at nine, the office Wi-Fi kept dropping, and the only free charger was across the room. Worse, the team chat kept pinging with Deepika's news: a conference talk, a client award. Rustam's own draft felt thin. The old habit whispered: compare. Instead, Rustam opened last year's appraisal. "Needs close supervision on client calls." This year Rustam had run eleven calls alone. That line went in first. Then Rustam muted the loud industry group that always left a sour taste and typed to Deepika: "Congrats on the talk! Could you show me how you structured it, sometime next week?" A thumbs-up came back 👍. At 8:52, the Wi-Fi held long enough to submit.

qa.q: How many client calls had Rustam run alone this year?
qa.a: Eleven calls.

qa.q: What did Rustam feel as Deepika's news kept pinging?
qa.a: Rustam felt insecure about the thin draft and was tugged by the old habit of measuring up against Deepika's achievements.

qa.q: What turning point shaped the appraisal, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: Opening last year's appraisal let Rustam measure against "needs close supervision" and lead with real growth, instead of against someone else's highlights.

qa.q: How might Deepika read Rustam's message?
qa.a: Deepika would likely feel appreciated rather than envied, since the message congratulates first and then asks to learn.

grounding: A young professional under deadline measures progress against last year, mutes a group that drags the mood down, and chooses to learn from one peer.
